Following established best practices, these models typically include a final normalization layer after all residual blocks. H-Net adopts this convention through network normalization, by placing an RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich 2019) at the end of each network component (Es, Ds, and M). This addition of a normalization layer addresses a critical challenge in hierarchical architectures. Pre-normalization allows residual stream magnitudes to grow unbounded through successive layers, with feature norms increasing monotonically. For H-Net, this poses a particular problem: the architecture leverages residual connections to preserve fine-grained information across stages. Without network normalization, outputs from deeper components (especially the many-layered main network) would dominate the residual signals from earlier encoder networks through imbalanced feature norms, neglecting the fine-grained details that are essential for decompression. The normalization layers restore balance between processed features and residual information, ensuring both contribute meaningfully to the final representation. Separation of Two Streams. Question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by the square root of d_k?

question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide by the square root of d_k?

result.text: Scaled dot‑product attention divides the raw dot products by the square root of the key dimension \(d_k\) to prevent the values from becoming too large. Large dot products push the softmax into regions with very small gradients, which hampers learning. Scaling by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the softmax input in a numerically stable range and improves training stability [2][1].

question: What is Inner Monologue in Moshi?

result.text: Inner Monologue is a training and inference procedure in Moshi that jointly models text and audio tokens, allowing the model to generate acoustic tokens alongside semantic tokens and thereby produce speech in real time. It enables Moshi to benefit from the knowledge of its Helium backbone and to generate a wide range of emotions, voices, and acoustic conditions. This approach also improves spoken question‑answering accuracy, almost tripling performance on benchmarks while only marginally increasing inference cost. [3][1]

dialogue system that aims at solving the aforementioned limitations: latency, textual information bottleneck and turn-based modeling. Moshi augments a text LLM backbone with a smaller audio language model (Borsos et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023) that ingests and predicts discrete audio units. This removes the information bottleneck of text by understanding inputs and generating outputs directly in the audio domain, while benefiting from the knowledge and reasoning abilities of the underlying text LLM. We extend previous work on audio language models and design a streaming, hierarchical architecture, with a theoretical latency of 160 ms—lower than the 230 ms average in natural conversations measured over 10 languages (Stivers et al., 2009).
